title: Internet Security Glossary, Version 2
summary: A large glossary of information security terms, abbreviations, and explanations, meant to help authors of Internet documents use security vocabulary consistently. It gives recommendations on choosing terms: reuse the same term for the same concept, prefer plain dictionary meanings, and avoid terms that favor a particular vendor. It is informational and a handy reference.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4949 defines security terms and explains how writers can use them consistently in Internet documents. Its recommendations are the author's views, not official IETF rules.

subtitle: A guide to consistent security vocabulary in Internet documents, with definitions and advice on when to use each term.

tldr.problem: Security documents can become harder to understand when writers use different terms for the same idea or give familiar terms different meanings.
tldr.mechanism: The glossary defines security terms and abbreviations, adds explanations and references, and labels entries I, N, O, or D to guide their use in Internet documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4949 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2828. Its terminology advice and some interpretations are the author's opinions, not an official IETF position.

today: RFC 4949 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2828. The RFC Editor note says its recommendations and some interpretations are the author's opinions, not an official IETF position.

sections.title: Why a Security Glossary
sections.content:
RFC 4949 collects definitions, abbreviations, explanations, and references for information system security terms. It calls RFCs, Internet-Drafts, and other discussion documents produced through the Internet Standards Process IDOCs.

The glossary aims to make those documents easier to understand. It recommends using the same term for the same idea, choosing familiar dictionary meanings and established terms, and avoiding wording that favors a vendor or one technology over competing approaches.

The introduction also notes that the glossary is biased toward English as used in the United States. Its coverage of government and defense terminology is limited to U.S. usage.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary helps writers use security terms consistently in RFCs and related Internet documents. It favors familiar wording and warns that its English and government terminology mainly reflects U.S. usage.

sections.title: How to Read an Entry
sections.content:
Entries are sorted alphabetically without regard to capitalization. Each entry begins with a dollar sign and a space, so a reader can search for $ term to find the defining entry instead of another mention of the term.

An entry may contain numbered definitions when a term has several meanings. The glossary places recommended meanings first, marks context-specific meanings, and uses notes such as Tutorial, Example, or Deprecated Usage to add guidance. Cross-references point to related or contrasting terms.

The glossary says its explanatory text may be reused in Internet documents, but it does not override wording already established in a document that uses the entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Look for the dollar sign and term to locate its definition. Numbered meanings, context labels, notes, and cross-references help explain how the word is being used.

sections.title: The Four Entry Types
sections.content:
Each entry is marked I, N, O, or D. The letter indicates the definition's origin and whether the glossary recommends using it in Internet documents.

  • I marks a recommended Internet-origin definition, or a generic definition the glossary can state without conflicting with another authority. A usage note may narrow where it applies.
  • N marks a recommended definition with a non-Internet origin. Use it only when needed and within any stated context or limit.
  • O marks a non-Internet definition that should not be used unless it is clearly identified as non-Internet.
  • D marks a deprecated term or definition that the glossary says should not be used. The entry gives a reason in a note.

When an older definition is too narrow or unsuitable, the glossary may mark it O and place a recommended I or N definition before it as a substitute.
sections.plainLanguage: The letter on an entry tells you whether the glossary recommends that writers use the term. I and N are recommended with different origins; O and D warn writers against using a definition without care.

sections.title: Threats, Vulnerabilities, Attacks, and Risk
sections.content:
The glossary separates security ideas that are often confused. A threat is a possible cause of harm. It may be intentional or accidental. A vulnerability is a weakness in a system's design, implementation, operation, or management that could let someone violate its security policy.

An attack is an intentional act that tries to evade security services and violate a system's security policy. The glossary uses threat action for the realization of a threat, whether through an intentional act or an accidental event, and warns that writers often misuse “threat” to mean either a threat action or a vulnerability.

Risk is the expectation of loss expressed as the probability that a threat will exploit a vulnerability and cause harm. The glossary describes four responses: avoid the risk by countering the threat or removing the weakness; transfer it to another system or entity; limit resulting loss with controls; or accept the potential loss and continue operating.
sections.plainLanguage:
A threat is a possible source of harm, while a vulnerability is a weakness that could be exploited. An attack is an intentional attempt to break security, and risk describes the chance of a harmful result.

The glossary lists ways to respond: remove the cause, shift the risk, reduce the loss, or accept the possible loss.

sections.title: Examples: Authentication and Signatures
sections.content:
The entries show how the glossary combines a definition with practical explanation. Authentication is checking a claim that a system entity or resource has a particular attribute. The glossary describes two steps: present the claimed attribute, then present or generate evidence that verifies the claimed link.

A digital signature is a value linked to data so a recipient can verify the data's origin and integrity. The tutorial describes making one by hashing the data and transforming the hash with the signer's private key; a recipient uses the corresponding public key to check it.

A public-key infrastructure (PKI) is a system that manages certificates, keys, archives, and related functions for users of asymmetric cryptography. The glossary lists registering users and issuing certificates, revoking certificates when needed, and keeping information that can help validate certificates later as core PKI functions.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication checks a claim about an identity or another attribute. A digital signature lets a recipient check who signed data and whether it changed. A public-key infrastructure (PKI) coordinates certificate and key management, including issuing and revoking certificates and keeping information for later checks.

sections.title: What the Glossary Does Not Cover
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section says the document mainly defines security terms and recommends how to use them. It also provides limited tutorial information about security aspects of Internet protocols.

It does not describe specific protocol vulnerabilities or threats in detail, and it does not definitively describe the mechanisms that protect specific protocols. Readers should treat it as a vocabulary reference, not a security analysis of an individual protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains security vocabulary and offers limited background about Internet protocols. It does not analyze the weaknesses of a particular protocol or fully describe that protocol's protections.

sections.title: Informational Advice, Not an IETF Position
sections.content:
RFC 4949 is an Informational memo and does not specify an Internet Standard. The RFC Editor note says the recommendations and some interpretations in its definitions are the author's opinions, not an official IETF position. It says the IETF has taken no formal position for or against the recommendations, so readers must judge whether to follow them.

The document is a major revision and expansion of the Security Glossary in RFC 2828, which RFC 4949 obsoletes. Its normative reference is RFC 2119, which defines the requirement words the glossary uses while warning that those words are unofficial in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 4949 is informational, and its recommendations reflect the author's views rather than an official IETF decision. It replaces the earlier security glossary in RFC 2828.

viz.caption: THE FOUR DEFINITION TYPES USED IN THE GLOSSARY

items.label: Recommended, Internet origin
items.desc: Recommended for Internet documents; a usage note may limit where it applies.

items.label: Recommended, non-Internet origin
items.desc: Recommended if needed, within any stated context or limit.

items.label: Other definition to note
items.desc: Do not use unless it is identified as non-Internet.

items.label: Deprecated
items.desc: The glossary says this term or definition SHOULD NOT be used.
